Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments

- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving
Violations
Kabir Dasgupta, Marco Francesconi, Jonathan James
Linda Kirkpatrick, and Alexander Plum*
October 29, 2026
Abstract
This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market out-
comes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a
staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after convic-
tion to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly
earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry
as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are
more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.
JEL Codes:K42, J24, J31, J15
Keywords:Drink-driving convictions, Criminal records and employment, Labour market
effects of crime, Administrative data and causal inference

1 Introduction
Imprisonment is often regarded as the most severe consequence of criminal activity. Yet,
many misdemeanours can bring about costs that extend beyond the courtroom. Drink-driving
1, a prevalent but often non-custodial offence, demonstrates this well: in the absence of
incarceration, convictions result in a criminal record, with lasting consequences on labour
market outcomes. This is most salient where background checks by employers are routine.
Several mechanisms may underpin these effects (Becker, 1968; Freeman, 1999). First,
the stigma associated with a criminal record can create substantial barriers to hiring and limit
access to employment opportunities (Uggen et al., 2014; Agan and Starr, 2017). Second, a
conviction may weaken attachment to the labour market by reducing incentives to seek or
retain employment (Visher et al., 2011; Sugie, 2018; Smith and Broege, 2020; Hjalmarsson
et al., 2024; Ramakers et al., 2025). Lastly, causality may also operate in the opposite direc-
tion: weaker labour market prospects may increase risky behaviours, such as heavy alcohol
consumption (MacDonald and Shields, 2001; Auld, 2005), thereby increasing the likelihood
of alcohol-related arrests and convictions.2 In this paper, we isolate and estimate the causal
effect of a drink-driving conviction on subsequent labour market outcomes in New Zealand.
We link administrative data from the Ministry of Justice court records, Inland Revenue
tax data, and the 2023 New Zealand Census to estimate the causal effect of a first-time drink-
driving conviction on employment and earnings. Our empirical strategy exploits variation
in the timing of conviction within a population of individuals who are all eventually con-
victed. We compare individuals before and after their first conviction with those convicted in
a later period using a staggered difference-in-differences design (Callaway and Sant’Anna,
2021). This avoids comparing offenders with non-offenders, since time-invariant differences
between the two groups could otherwise confound the relationship between conviction and
labour market outcomes. In our approach, both treatment and comparison groups are drawn
from the same population of eventual offenders, differing only in the timing of conviction.
We complement this design with an exact matching approach, comparing convicted individ-
uals to observationally similar members of the general public who do not receive a court
conviction during the sample period.
1We follow the terminology used by the New Zealand Transport Agency and refer to this offence as “drink-
driving” throughout the paper, consistent with usage in New Zealand and other Commonwealth jurisdictions.
In the United States, the equivalent offence is typically referred to as “drunk driving” or “driving under the
influence (DUI).
2A related literature examines the direct relationship between alcohol consumption and labour market out-
comes (Berger and Leigh, 1988; Zarkin et al., 1998; MacDonald and Shields, 2001, 2004; Auld, 2005).
1
Drink-driving convictions in New Zealand are ideally suited for examining the informa-
tional consequences of criminal records. They are often non-custodial, involving fines or
temporary licence suspensions rather than imprisonment. Thus, our estimates abstract away
from incapacitation and human capital depreciation that occur during incarceration. Drink-
driving offences are also well suited to this design because severity is measured using breath
or blood alcohol readings, which provide an objective and continuous measure of the offence
that maps onto clear legal thresholds. This distinguishes drink-driving from many other mis-
demeanours, where severity may be more difficult to measure consistently (Sherman et al.,
2016). Furthermore, individuals may be uncertain about their precise alcohol concentration
at the time of driving (Love and Larue, 2025), meaning small measured differences in alcohol
concentration can translate into different legal outcomes. The availability of recorded alco-
hol readings allows us to construct a homogeneous analysis sample of first-time offenders
with readings in a narrow range at the lower end of the conviction distribution, all receiving
similar non-custodial penalties. This restriction is important: it allows us to focus on the ef-
fect of acquiring a criminal record among similar low-level offenders, avoiding comparisons
between individuals who differ substantially in offence severity or punishment.
Given the prevalence of such convictions, understanding their labour market conse-
quences is of clear importance. Linking the 2023 New Zealand Census to Ministry of Justice
court charge records, we find that 15.3% of men and 5.8% of women aged 30–55 have at least
one drink-driving conviction. Among those with a drink-driving conviction, 25.1% of men
and 43.9% of women have only a single recorded conviction. This suggests that drink-driving
convictions are relatively common among individuals with otherwise limited criminal his-
tories. These offences largely fall into the category ofsummary offences, the New Zealand
equivalent of misdemeanours, which are adjudicated without a jury and typically involve
non-custodial penalties. Internationally, comparable offence classes account for the majority
of criminal cases carried out in common-law jurisdictions.3 Despite their prevalence, lower-
level offences such as drink-driving have received relatively little attention in the literature,
which has instead focused disproportionately on incarceration and more serious crimes (for
an important exception, see Agan et al., 2023).
3For example, in England and Wales, summary offences account for around 90% of all criminal cases han-
dled by magistrates’ courts (Ministry of Justice, 2023). In Canada, most completed adult criminal court cases
involve summary conviction offences rather than indictable crimes (Department of Justice Canada, 2023). Sim-
ilarly, in Australia, the bulk of defendants finalised in criminal courts are charged with non-indictable offences
(Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2023). In the United States, misdemeanours account for the vast majority
of criminal filings in state courts (Stevenson and Mayson, 2018), and population-level estimates suggest that
roughly one in seven Americans have been convicted of a misdemeanour at some point in their lives (Craigie
et al., 2020).
2
In contrast to an extensive literature on deterrence and road safety (Dee, 2001; Eisen-
berg, 2003; Albalate, 2008; Francesconi and James, 2021; Portillo et al., 2024; Ramasco,
2026), a small body of non-economic research on the consequences of drink-driving con-
victions documents negligible labour market impacts. Early studies have focused on the ef-
fects of licence suspension or revocation on employment outcomes. Wells-Parker and Cosby
(1988) used telephone surveys to compare 416 suspended and non-suspended DUI (driving
under the influence) offenders in Mississippi, United State and found limited evidence of
an effect on employment.4 Similarly, Knoebel and Ross (1997) surveyed 579 first-time and
233 repeat-DUI offenders across several US jurisdictions with differing licence revocation
regimes and reported minimal impacts on job status and income. The reliance on small,
self-reported survey data, however, limits the credibility of the estimates in these studies.
More recent work has used administrative data to examine broader economic outcomes
following drink-driving convictions. Using Finnish register data, Oksanen et al. (2015) show
that individuals are more likely to experience debt problems, divorce, and face an income
loss of approximately 20%, three years following their first offence. While this study ex-
ploits within-individual variation over time, it remains largely descriptive, lacking a formal
identification strategy and failing to account for pre-existing trends.
Our study also contributes to a growing economic literature examining how criminal
justice contact affects labour market outcomes through the information conveyed by a crim-
inal record itself (Finlay, 2009; Agan and Starr, 2017). A key finding in this literature is
that employers respond to information about criminal history, though effects are often het-
erogeneous and context-dependent. Evidence from field experiments shows that criminal
records reduce callback rates for job applicants. Concurrently, policies that restrict access
to information, such as “Ban-the-Box”, can alter employer screening in ways that generate
unintended consequences, including increased statistical discrimination against minority ap-
plicants (Agan and Starr, 2018). Subsequent research has shown considerable heterogeneity
in Ban-the-Box employment effects across data sources, institutional settings, and popula-
tion subgroups, yielding inconclusive evidence on aggregate employment impacts (Craigie,
2020; Doleac and Hansen, 2020; Shoag and Veuger, 2021; Rose, 2021; Burton and Wasser,
2025).
Related evidence from “clean slate” and record-remediation reforms, which conceal,
clear or reduce the severity of criminal records after a period without reoffending, also
points to modest earnings gains among the employed. However, the evidence on overall
4This null result can be partly explained by offenders still driving when suspended.
3
employment rates is weak (Dasgupta et al., 2025; Agan et al., 2024a,b). One interpretation
is that criminal records may scar labour-market trajectories soon after contact with the crim-
inal justice system, leading to employment disparities or movement into lower-opportunity
jobs that are difficult to rectify later. Overall, the evidence shows that criminal records are
economically consequential, but the effects of revealing or concealing this information are
theoretically ambiguous and empirically mixed.5
The broader economic literature on criminal justice contact primarily focuses on incar-
ceration or pre-trial detention. These studies often exploit quasi-experimental variation, such
as random judge assignment or sentencing thresholds, to estimate causal effects on employ-
ment and earnings. The evidence is mixed – some studies find sentence length has little
impact on post-release labour market outcomes (Kling, 2006), while others document more
persistent employment and earnings losses following incarceration, especially for those with
strong pre-arrest labour market attachment (Mueller-Smith, 2015). 6 Pre-trial detention re-
duces formal-sector employment and being in receipt of government benefits (Dobbie et al.,
2018), with similar evidence from Chile showing that pre-trial detention lowers formal em-
ployment and monthly wages (Grau et al., 2023). More recent evidence using large admin-
istrative datasets suggests a substantial share of observed earnings losses associated with
incarceration reflects incapacitation and weak pre-existing labour market attachment, rather
than long-run scarring, once time spent incarcerated is accounted for (Garin et al., 2025).
This literature is important but is less directly relevant to settings such as ours, where the
offence does not typically result in imprisonment.
This paper makes three contributions. First, it provides the first causal evidence on the
impact of drink-driving convictions on labour market outcomes, focusing on employment
and earnings rather than road safety or recidivism. We identify the economic consequences
of a criminal conviction by examining non-custodial drink-driving offences, exploiting new
linked administrative data that combine detailed court records, including recorded breath
alcohol levels, with earnings data. This setting allows us to abstract from imprisonment
and variation in sentencing severity, and to trace labour market trajectories before and after
conviction.
Second, we implement an identification strategy based on variation in the timing of in-
dividuals’ first drink-driving conviction. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design
5Relatedly, Mueller-Smith and Schnepel (2021) find that avoiding a conviction has a significantly positive
impact on labour market outcomes.
6Mueller-Smith (2015) finds that each additional year of incarceration reduces post-release employment by
3.6 percentage points and significantly lowers earnings by 0.34 log points. Among misdemeanour defendants,
imprisonment reduces employment by 4.5 percentage points and earnings by 0.42 log points.
4
and a control group of individuals who are convicted in the future (Callaway and Sant’Anna,
2021), we estimate treatment effects within a population of individuals who eventually inter-
act with the criminal justice system. Conditioning on eventual conviction mitigates concerns
that unobserved characteristics drive both the propensity to offend and labour market attach-
ment. We then implement an exact matching design combined with a fixed effects event-
study specification, comparing convicted individuals to observationally similar individuals
with no recorded court conviction during the sample period. The results are similar using
both approaches, indicating that our estimates are not an artifact of the choice of control
group.
To further ensure our treatment and control groups are comparable, we restrict the sam-
ple to offenders at the lower end of the breath/blood alcohol distribution. Our sample in-
cludes those with readings of 500 micrograms of alcohol per litre or less, accounting for
15% of all offenders. These individuals are closer to the legal conviction threshold, making
them more comparable to drivers with readings just below the threshold. In New Zealand,
a summary drink-driving offence applies for readings between 400 and 800 micrograms of
alcohol per litre of breath.7 By comparison, the mean reading among all convicted offenders
in our data is 650 micrograms, indicating that the typical offender is substantially further
away from the threshold.
Third, we find meaningful labour market effects following conviction that persist over
time. Employment falls by 6–7 percentage points on average, while monthly earnings fall
by NZ$90 (around 2% at baseline). These effects are driven by both reduced entry into
employment and increased job loss, with the larger effect operating through reduced job-
finding among the unemployed. Further, we find that impacts on employment are larger in
industries with a high propensity to screen applicants for criminal convictions. This pattern is
consistent with evidence from Agan and Starr (2017), who show job applicants with criminal
records face substantially lower callback rates than those without. Moreover, the effects
persist beyond the typical six-month licence suspension period, suggesting that short-term
driving restrictions are unlikely to explain the results. We capture the essential elements of
our findings in a simple model of employer screening in a frictional labour market, which we
present in the penultimate section. This framework shows that convictions reduce perceived
productivity by employers, resulting in a hiring penalty that disproportionately affects job
entry relative to job retention.

2 Institutional Background
Figure 1 summarises the evolution of New Zealand’s drink-driving regime. The figure plots
the share of alcohol-related road casualties alongside selected policy changes affecting al-
cohol testing, legal drink-driving limits, and punishments. Over the period shown, New
Zealand progressively strengthened its drink-driving enforcement through evidential and ran-
dom breath testing (1988, 1993), lower legal alcohol limits (1998, 2011, 2014), and manda-
tory interlocks for repeat offenders (2018). Alcohol-related casualties declined substantially
over this period, although drink-driving remains an important road-safety concern.8

drink-driving policy changes. Vertical dashed lines indicate major changes to alcohol testing, legal
thresholds, and sanctions.
The legal consequences of drink-driving are determined by the degree to which a driver’s
blood or breath alcohol concentration exceeds statutory limits. The Land Transport Act
8We use the figure to describe the institutional setting rather than as a source of identifying variation.
6
1998 provides the core legal framework governing alcohol-impaired driving and associated
penalties, and has been amended over time to address alcohol-related road-safety risks (New
Zealand Government, 2026). Two features of this framework are central to our analysis.
First, alcohol concentration is measured using standardised breath or blood tests, generating
an objective and continuous measure of alcohol impairment. Second, legal consequences
depend on thresholds, where lower-level breaches are treated as infringement offences and
higher-level breaches are prosecuted in court. The court-prosecution threshold is important
as it is the point at which a drink-driving incident can generate a formal criminal conviction.
Enforcement relies on widespread roadside checks, with police authorised to stop drivers
and administer alcohol tests without requiring reasonable suspicion. Four types of tests are
used to assess alcohol impairment (Controller and Auditor General, 2013): (i)passive breath
tests, an initial roadside screening using a handheld device to detect the presence of alcohol;
(ii)breath screening tests, administered if the driver fails or refuses the passive test, where
failing the screening test determines whether further evidential testing is required;9 (iii)evi-
dential breath tests, which provide a court-admissible measure of breath alcohol concentra-
tion; and (iv)evidential blood tests, conducted by a health professional if breath testing is
refused or failed. Courts typically prioritise evidential breath or blood results when deter-
mining whether an offence has occurred and the relevant penalty.
At the time of its introduction, the Land Transport Act set the legal blood alcohol con-
centration (BAC) limit at 30 mg per 100 ml of blood, or 150 micrograms (µg) per litre of
breath, for drivers under 20, and 80 mg per 100 ml of blood, or 400µg per litre of breath,
for drivers aged 20 and over. 10 Exceeding these limits resulted in court-imposed penalties,
including fines, licence suspension, or imprisonment. In 1999, the legal alcohol purchasing
age was reduced from 20 to 18 (Kypri et al., 2006), increasing access to, and consumption
of, alcohol among young adults (Boes and Stillman, 2013; Dasgupta et al., 2022).
In 2011, a zero-alcohol policy was introduced for drivers under 20, replacing the previ-
ous youth limit of 30 mg per 100 ml of blood, or 150µg per litre of breath (New Zealand
Government, 2026). Under the new regime, driving with any measurable alcohol became
unlawful for drivers under 20. However, the penalties were tiered. Low-level breaches be-

Based on Table 4 above, individuals with any conviction history experience significantly
lower employment probabilities compared to those with no convictions in the past. Convic-
tions that led to custodial sentences (like imprisonment or home detention) have the strongest
negative effect, with reductions in the probability of being employed ranging from 2.4 to 5.4
percentage points across the three time periods post-Census. Non-traffic convictions with
less severe sentences such as community work or monetary penalties appear to have compa-
rable magnitudes, with effects varying between 2.2 and 4.7 percentage points. Meanwhile,
traffic violations that led to community sentences or monetary fines show somewhat smaller
but statistically significant declines in the employment probability in the range of 1.3-1.7 per-
centage points. In general, our results are aligned with the survey-based findings discussed
above. Importantly, all estimates are statistically significant and relatively stable across the
observation periods, suggesting persistent employment penalties associated with criminal
justice involvement, regardless of offense severity.
Screening intensity and driving requirements— To further examine the extent that screen-
ing plays in the formulation of new employment matches we categorise industries by the
extent that criminal records are screened during the recruitment process. We do not have
direct measures of screening behaviour however we reviewed each ANZSIC 2006 division-
subdivision and assigned it to low-, medium-, or high-screening likelihood based on industry
characteristics. Features of industries that make screening more likely include formal regu-
lation, safety-sensitive tasks, responsibility for vulnerable populations, public trust, or unsu-
pervised access to clients. Appendix Table B.4 presents the results. It shows that, following
conviction, employment through new matches falls by 1.9 percentage points in industries
with a low probability to screen and by 4.8 percentage points for medium to high screening
industries. This evidence is consistent with the conviction acting as a negative signal to em-
ployers at the hiring stage, and this signal is obviously more salient and apparent in those
industries that screen.
Relatedly, we also examine whether the effects are concentrated in industries where
driving is a key part of the job. If the results are a function of workers not being able to per-
form key (driving parts) of their job, then one would expect the effects to be concentrated in

those industries. In contrast to this hypothesis, Appendix Table B.5 shows that employment
through new matches falls by 4.9 percentage points in low-driving-requirement industries,
compared with 1.9 percentage points in high-driving industries. This evidence then provides
little support that the decline in employment is being driven primarily licence loss.

Implications. The model yields three main predictions. First, employment declines follow-
ing a conviction because employer screening lowers the probability that a new match satisfies
the hiring condition (10), as implied by Equations (6) and (9). Second, the effect operates
primarily through reduced entry into employment rather than increased separations. This is
because criminal records are used primarily during hiring, whereas after a match forms em-
ployers increasingly rely on direct observations of worker performance. As employer learn-
ing replaces pre-hiring signals (Equation (11)), the informational value of a criminal record
diminishes, reducing its influence on retention decisions. Third, conditional on employment,
wage effects are comparatively modest. This follows from the wage-setting Equation (8)
together with the positive selection induced by the hiring threshold in Equation (10), which
raises average productivity among employed convicted workers (see Equation (13)).
These predictions align closely with our empirical findings, which show a substantial
decline in employment driven primarily by reduced entry into employment, comparatively
small increases in separations, and relatively modest effects on labour income.25

In this environment, a criminal conviction affects labour market outcomes through three
channels. First, it reduces expected productivity, tightening the hiring condition and lowering
employment entry (the screening channel). Second, because convicted workers who are hired
are positively selected, average match quality among employed workers is higher, which
helps explain why separations remain limited even in the presence of sizeable employment
effects. Third, convictions may weaken workers’ outside options and mobility across firms,

These mechanisms jointly shape wage determination. In particular, wages reflect (i)
productivity-based screening through lower expected match quality, (ii) selection into em-

employment effects not only in magnitude but also in interpretation, since they embed both
composition effects and changes in employer wage-setting power.
A key implication of this extension is a sharper conceptual distinction between margins
of adjustment. Employment effects remain primarily driven by screening at the hiring stage,
whereas wage effects may additionally reflect employer market power over workers with
criminal records. This distinction also affects the interpretation of our estimates: while the
combination of large employment effects and more modest wage responses is consistent with
screening-based models, the presence of monopsony power implies that wage effects may
arise even in the absence of productivity losses. Consequently, the relatively small wage
effects we estimate can be interpreted as a lower bound on the true extent of labour-market
stigma associated with a conviction.
5 Conclusion
In this paper we find that decreased employment following a drink-driving conviction is
primarily driven by a lower likelihood of entering employment. This indicates that such a
conviction is negatively updated by employers and operates as a barrier to job access. By
contrast, for individuals already employed, we find only small effects on job retention and
labour income, suggesting that the main margin of adjustment is labour market entry rather
than within-job outcomes.
Heterogeneity analysis reveals systematic differences in labour market responses by eth-
nicity and gender. Non-Europeans experience larger declines in employment and earnings
than Europeans. This difference is driven by both lower entry into employment and higher
exit rates. While these patterns are not statistically distinguishable, they are suggestive of
heterogeneous penalties that may reflect differences in how misdemeanor convictions are
processed in employer screening and hiring decisions. Men and women experience compa-
rable overall employment declines, but the underlying margins differ. Reduced entry is the
primary channel for men. For women both reduced entry and increased exit contribute.
These empirical patterns are consistent with the mechanism emphasised in our concep-
tual framework, in which a misdemeanor conviction lowers expected match value. It reduces
30
the probability that a match is formed in a frictional labour market. Given that a convic-
tion primarily affects employers’ hiring decisions rather than the productivity of incumbent
workers, the model predicts that employment entry should be the key adjustment margin,
with comparatively smaller effects on separations and wages.
Policy implications follow directly from this mechanism. Since the main cost of a drink-
driving conviction operates through reduced employment entry, with disproportionate effects
for non-European individuals and, through higher exit rates, for women, these findings point
to several areas where further research and policy evaluation may be warranted.
First, examining whether a clearer distinction between low-level and more serious crim-
inal offending in DUI enforcement—through non-conviction or diversionary pathways for
borderline misdemeanor cases—affects labour market outcomes would be valuable. Al-
though current thresholds already differentiate sanctions by alcohol levels in most countries,
future research could investigate whether a greater emphasis on non-conviction resolutions
where public safety risk is limited reduces employment penalties while maintaining deter-
rence. This possibility aligns with recent evidence finding that avoiding formal prosecution
can mitigate re-offending and prevent longer-term harms (Agan et al., 2023). However, our
findings suggest that such approaches alone would likely be insufficient to address the full
scope of employment barriers.
Second, examining modifications to existing Clean Slate schemes that could allow el-
igible individuals to withhold low-level convictions from employers may be particularly
relevant for minor traffic offences. Our results suggest that the main effects arise through
reduced re-entry into employment rather than lower earnings among incumbent workers,
suggesting that shorter waiting periods or fewer exceptions may help reduce the long-term
employment consequences of these convictions.
Third, fair-chance hiring approaches that limit initial access to criminal record infor-
mation during hiring may affect employment opportunities for individuals with low-level
criminal records. However, existing research suggests that limiting access to criminal-record
information can also encourage employers to rely more heavily on other observable char-
acteristics when making hiring decisions. Alternative approaches such as targeted hiring
incentives or time-limited record disclosure may therefore complement efforts to reduce the
consequences of prosecution.
More broadly, the evidence from this study indicates that even relatively minor misde-
meanor convictions can generate persistent labour-market effects through employer screen-
ing rather than through incapacitation or human capital loss. These effects arise because con-
31
viction records continue to shape hiring decisions well beyond the period of formal sanction.
Our findings indicate that approaches focused solely on reducing prosecution of marginal
cases, while valuable, would leave already-convicted individuals exposed to persistent barri-
ers, underscoring the potential relevance of complementary approaches that facilitate labour-
market reintegration and their empirical evaluation.
